newsitem.title: USA: A president on crutches goes to New York.
newsitem.headline: A president on crutches goes to New York.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Tuesday ventured out of Washington for only the second time since knee surgery a month ago, and seemed to be bearing up about as well as could be expected.

Clinton travelled to New York City on Tuesday where, among other things, he was to attend a baseball game. He tore the right knee tendon at the Florida estate of golf pro Greg Norman on March 14 and underwent surgery the same day to repair it.

Instead of being loaded into a catering truck to be put on Air Force One on Tuesday, as he did March 19 when he travelled to Helsinki, Finland, Clinton was able to use his crutches for a slow, methodical climb up the plane's steps.
The usually active, vigorous Clinton was still getting around after the surgery, but at a much slower pace than before the injury.

He did not use the Marine One helicopter on Tuesday, because there is not much space for his extended leg to get comfortable, so he travelled to Andrews Air Force Base from the White House in a limousine and then was driven around New York by motorcade.

On his arrival at John F. Kennedy airport, Clinton's limousine pulled up within a few yards of the plane. He walked down the stairs braced by a crutch on his right arm and holding the railing with his left hand.
At the bottom of the stairs he took both crutches, flashed a smile at reporters and walked to his waiting car.

After speaking to a Brooklyn junior high school gathering then speaking to a Democratic fund-raiser, Clinton rested at a hotel near Shea Stadium, ahead of his appearance at Tuesday night's events marking the 50th anniversary of Jackie Robinson's breaking of the colour barrier in major league baseball.
During the down time, Navy Commander Bob Kellogg helped work the president through some physical therapy for his leg.
"He's fine. The therapy will do him some good, though," said a White House spokesman Barry Toiv. "It's a lot of activity and there's more tonight, so it'll do him some good."
